ceviri.26: How long does it take to set up a website chatbot?
ceviri.27: It varies with scope, but it helps to think in two stages. The technical setup — getting the assistant onto the site and working — usually takes a few days. The real time goes into the knowledge base: deciding which questions it will answer, gathering the source texts and writing the boundary can take one to two weeks. The best way to shorten that second stage is to collect the real questions coming in for a week before setup. With a list of real questions in hand, the scope discussion stops being guesswork.
ceviri.28: What happens if it gives out wrong information?
ceviri.29: The responsibility stays with the site's owner.
ceviri.30: Do visitors want to speak to a human?
ceviri.31: Some do, and blocking that request is the biggest mistake you can make. When the hand-over button is visible, most visitors choose to try the assistant first.
ceviri.32: Should we say the assistant isn't a human?
ceviri.33: Say it. Being open about it builds trust and sets the right expectation; hiding it backfires the moment it's noticed.
ceviri.34: If we don't publish prices on the site, should the assistant give them?
ceviri.35: No. The assistant shouldn't step outside the site's policy; it's better for it to explain the scope and point towards a quote conversation.
ceviri.36: Does it cause a problem if it collects personal data?
ceviri.37: If you're collecting a name, a phone number and an email address, the privacy notice and the retention period have to be defined. Settle that before setup.
ceviri.38: How often should I update the knowledge base?
ceviri.39: Whenever the site content changes. Beyond that, reading the list of unanswered questions once a month and closing the gaps is a good habit.
ceviri.40: Can it work in more than one language?
ceviri.41: It can; each language needs its own source text.

ceviri.55: What Does Adding a Chatbot to Your Website Change?
ceviri.56: Putting an assistant on the site is easy; getting it to work properly afterwards is hard. Most setups open with enthusiasm in the first month and are quietly switched off in the second. The reason is usually not the tool but the scope. In this piece we cover what it changes, where it should stop, and how you measure success. We're not giving figures like conversion rates; we don't write what we haven't measured.
ceviri.57: If the same question comes in dozens of times a day, writing the answer once is enough.
ceviri.59: What Does Setting Up a Website Chatbot Change?
ceviri.60: Three things: response time, the load of repeat questions, and the visitor's reason for staying on the page. When you set up a website chatbot, your team stops answering the same question ten times a day. The visitor gets the answer without waiting. The one thing that doesn't change is the damage done if you give out wrong information. That damage can outweigh the speed you gain.
ceviri.61: The most concrete gain is in the repeat questions. Opening hours, delivery times, service scope and pricing policy come round again every day; writing them once frees up the team's day.
ceviri.62: The second gain is in timing. If a question that arrives at midnight waits until morning, the visitor has usually looked elsewhere in the meantime. A site assistant closes that gap.
ceviri.63: Fewer people notice the third gain. The team stops repeating the same answer. The time left over goes to the questions that are genuinely new. The gain in productivity shows up not in a number but in where the attention goes.
ceviri.65: No. On a site that takes a few questions a day, the setup and upkeep outweigh the gain. When you set up a chatbot, look at your website's real question volume; don't decide on a guess.
ceviri.67: Only the ones it knows. Headings with a clear answer — price range, opening hours, delivery time, service scope — are safe ground. If a website chatbot guesses at something it doesn't know, it has made a false promise on your brand's behalf. Narrowing the boundary is worth more than widening the scope. An assistant that says it doesn't know beats an assistant that invents.
ceviri.68: Set the answer boundary down in writing. Put on a list which headings are inside and which are outside; with no list, there is no boundary.
ceviri.69: The four headings below sit in the safe zone on most sites.
ceviri.71: — what you do and what you don't.
ceviri.73: — how the work moves and how long it takes.
ceviri.75: — who to reach, how, and at what hours.
ceviri.77: — answers already written on the site.
ceviri.78: Prepare a single answer for the questions that fall outside the boundary. Let the assistant say it doesn't know and point at the right door. That one sentence does far better work than an invented answer. And the visitor knows where to go.
ceviri.79: Should It Answer the Price Question?
ceviri.80: Let it say whatever your policy is. If you give a clear range, the range; if it varies with scope, let it say so plainly. A vague answer pushes the visitor away from asking for a quote.
ceviri.81: When Should It Hand Over to a Human?
ceviri.82: In three situations. When the question moves outside the scope, when the visitor insists on a human, and when the conversation stalls for the second time. Show the hand-over button on every screen. If a website chatbot locks the visitor in, it takes back far more than the time it saved. Setting the hand-over moment early is easier than rescuing the conversation. A visitor who gets stuck doesn't come back.
ceviri.83: Handing over to a human isn't a failure; it's part of the design. A visitor doesn't get angry at not getting an answer; they get angry at not finding a way out.
ceviri.84: Pass the conversation history over with the hand-over. A visitor forced to explain the same thing a second time takes back far more than the time the assistant saved. We covered the relationship between user behaviour and interface decisions in the
ceviri.87: What Should Happen After the Hand-Over?
ceviri.88: Promise a response time. “As soon as possible” says nothing; “within two working days” sets the expectation. Don't write a time you can't keep; a broken promise is worse than no promise at all.
ceviri.89: How Do You Build the Knowledge Base?
ceviri.90: The source texts come out of your own site's pages. Service descriptions, frequently asked questions and pricing policy texts are the soundest source. When a website chatbot stays inside those texts, the risk of a wrong answer drops. Put updating the source on the calendar too; a text that goes stale means an answer that goes stale.
ceviri.91: Gathering the source texts brings you one more advantage: the pages that were written thinly come to light. Every question the assistant can't answer actually points at a heading missing from your site.
ceviri.92: That's why we build the knowledge base not as a separate document outside the site but as an extension of the site's own content. When the content is updated, the answer is updated. We set out what that looks like on the interface side in the
ceviri.95: Keep the source texts short and clear. Long pages heavy with marketing language make the assistant speak vaguely too. Writing what you do in plain sentences helps the visitor and the assistant alike. Chat logs are personal data;
ceviri.97: applies to chatbots too; KVKK is Türkiye's data protection law.
ceviri.99: A few right pages beat many scattered ones. On most sites the service pages and the FAQs make a sufficient start.
ceviri.100: “A visitor doesn't get angry at not getting an answer; they get angry at not finding a way out. Show the hand-over door on every screen.”
ceviri.103: Look at four numbers. The number of conversations, the hand-over rate, the number of unanswered questions, and the enquiries that come out of conversations. The last one matters most; the other three serve it. Measuring a website chatbot's success by conversation count misleads. Nobody comes to your site to talk to an assistant. People come to get something done.
ceviri.104: The breakdown of unanswered questions is the most valuable output. That list gives you the route map for both the knowledge base and the site content; it's the one report worth reading every month.
ceviri.105: Don't take the hand-over rate as good or bad on its own either. A high rate can mean the scope is too narrow; a very low one can suggest the assistant isn't letting the visitor go. Read both alongside the unanswered-question list.
ceviri.106: Start measuring from the first month. The first week after setup is usually atypical; the team tries out its own assistant and the numbers inflate. The real trend settles from the second month. Early decisions usually turn out wrong.
ceviri.107: Let's Set Up Your Own Assistant Together
ceviri.108: Drawing the scope together is the quickest route. We talk through which questions it will answer, where it will hand over to a human, and what will feed the knowledge base. What you're left with isn't the name of a tool but a scope in writing. When a website chatbot is set up with that scope, it saves your team time instead of adding to their load. An assistant set up without a scope gets switched off in the second month.
ceviri.109: We'd suggest collecting questions for a week before the setup. Real questions always give a better starting point than an estimated scope.
ceviri.113: are the pages to look at next.
ceviri.114: We build the chatbot not as a plugin on your website but as your content speaking. If the content is good the assistant is good; if the content has gaps, the assistant magnifies them.
ceviri.115: While you're writing the scope, set a stopping criterion too. Decide at the outset which number you'd need to see after three months to carry on. Every tool set up without a criterion stays switched on for years because nobody can decide. The stopping criterion matters as much as the setup.
ceviri.116: Don't hide the hand-over door; a visitor who gets stuck doesn't come back.

_kararlar.odak kelime → website chatbot: Türkçe metin 'web sitesi chatbot' öbeğini tekrar ediyor (odak kelime). İngilizcede karşılığı 'website chatbot'; slug da bundan türedi.
_kararlar.insana devir → hand-over: Britanya yazımında tireli 'hand-over' (isim). 'Escalation' çağrı merkezi jargonu, sayfa sade dil kullanıyor.
_kararlar.aydınlatma metni → privacy notice: KVKK'nın 'aydınlatma metni' yükümlülüğünün İngilizce karşılığı; GDPR literatüründe de 'privacy notice'.
_kararlar.96/97 KVKK: Sözlük kuralı: kısaltma korunur, yanına açıklama eklenir. Bağlantı metni kısa tutuldu ('KVKK's disclosure obligation'), açıklama sonraki kayda taşındı — İngilizce okur hangi ülkenin mevzuatı olduğunu bilmiyor.
_kararlar.1/9 başlık farkı: Kayıt 1 (title) 'What Does Adding a Chatbot to Your Website Change? | TasarımMania' olsaydı 64 karakter, sınır 60. Title kısaltıldı; H1 ve şema başlığı BASLIK sözlüğündeki hâliyle kaldı — hizmet sayfalarındaki 'ilgili yazılar' kartları o başlığı kullanıyor, ikisi ayrışmamalı.
_kararlar.84-86 / 92-94 / 110-113 bölünmüş cümlele: Bağlantı metni cümlenin ortasında ve Türkçe söz dizimi sona yüklem koyuyor. İngilizcede cümle yeniden kuruldu, kayıt sınırları korundu: '...in the' + '<link>' + ' piece.'
_kararlar.100 HTML varlıkları: Türkçe kayıt “ ve ” varlıklarını METİN olarak taşıyor; İngilizcede de aynen bırakıldı, yoksa tırnak biçimi bozulur.
_kararlar.123/126 'Evet' · 129/132 'Hayır' · 135/1: Aynı Türkçe dizge iki kez geçiyor; çakışma kilidi gereği ikisi de aynı İngilizce.
_kararlar.107/140 büyük-küçük harf farkı: Türkçede biri başlık düzeni, biri cümle düzeni — İngilizcede de fark korundu.
